facts.text: Multi-simulator architecture spreads a test program across several simulation fidelity levels and tools, each used for the questions it answers well, rather than running every case in one maximum-fidelity simulator.
facts.quote: spread the test program across several levels of simulation fidelity and several tools, each used for the questions it answers well, instead of running every case in one maximum-fidelity simulator

facts.text: The booklet recommends a multi-simulator alternative called the "fourth architecture", which is valid at any cost level.
facts.quote: The booklet calls the alternative a "fourth architecture", valid at any cost level [Chapter 11]

facts.text: The fourth architecture uses deterministic functional and object-list tests for millions of braking-logic combinations.
facts.quote: Deterministic functional and object-list tests for millions of braking-logic combinations.

facts.text: The fourth architecture uses medium-fidelity closed-loop dynamics with ideal or noisy sensors for broad regression testing.
facts.quote: Medium-fidelity closed-loop dynamics with ideal or noisy sensors for broad regression.

facts.text: The fourth architecture reserves high-fidelity rendering, radar and lidar simulation for perception-sensitive subsets of tests.
facts.quote: High-fidelity rendering, radar and lidar for perception-sensitive subsets.

facts.text: The fourth architecture reserves high-fidelity soil simulation for braking- and traction-sensitive subsets of tests.
facts.quote: High-fidelity soil simulation for braking- and traction-sensitive subsets.

facts.text: The fourth architecture uses hardware-in-the-loop testing for timing, controller and interface behavior.
facts.quote: Hardware-in-the-loop for timing, controller and interface behavior.

facts.text: The fourth architecture uses targeted physical tests for correlation and final evidence.
facts.quote: Targeted physical tests for correlation and final evidence.

facts.text: Allocation of test cases to each simulation fidelity level must be based on sensitivity and correlation work, not assumption.
facts.quote: The allocation of cases to each level must come from sensitivity and correlation work, not from assumption

facts.text: The simulation-tool market is modular: road-vehicle tools are strong in sensors and scenarios, while heavy-machine tools are strong in terrain and hydraulics; the booklet states that nobody has both.
facts.quote: The market itself is modular, with road-vehicle tools strong in sensors and scenarios and heavy-machine tools strong in terrain and hydraulics, and nobody has both [Chapter 11].

facts.text: High-fidelity soil simulation runs 50 to 200 times slower than real time and cannot be used for every regression case.
facts.quote: High-fidelity soil runs 50 to 200 times slower than real time and cannot be used for every regression case [Chapter 11].

facts.text: The GPU-hour ceiling within a four-month validation window limits the number of full-fidelity simulation runs.
facts.quote: The GPU-hour ceiling of a four-month window caps full-fidelity runs [Chapter 11].

facts.text: Simulation fidelity should be decomposed according to the requirement being tested rather than ranked by how convincing simulator screenshots look.
facts.quote: fidelity should be decomposed by the tested requirement rather than ranked by how convincing the screenshots look [Chapter 5].

facts.text: The booklet recommends layered models for each machine family rather than one "ultimate" digital twin.
facts.quote: layered models per machine family rather than one "ultimate" digital twin [Chapter 8].

facts.text: Multi-simulator architecture requires integration work; open standards reduce that work but do not remove it.
facts.quote: The price is integration work, which open standards reduce but do not remove [Chapter 11].

facts.text: Multi-simulator architecture enables a program starting from zero to cover the combinatorial test space within the available window while reserving scarce high-fidelity simulation and physical-test resources for cases where correlation shows they are needed.
facts.quote: This architecture is how a program starting from zero can cover the combinatorial space inside the window while spending its scarce high-fidelity and physical resources only where correlation shows they are needed [Chapter 11].
